name: Double eyelid suture (non-incisional)

lead: The non-incisional double eyelid method creates an upper-lid crease with buried stitches instead of a cut, giving larger, more defined eyes to people who lack a crease. It is a common East Asian aesthetic procedure and is described as quicker than the incisional approach.

Sutures passed through the lid bind the skin to deeper tissue such as the levator aponeurosis, so a fold forms when the eye opens. The new crease is visible straight away. Encyclopedia summaries say it is associated with fewer complications than the incisional approach but that the crease can be static and may fade. Published work is retrospective, including large cohorts on crease loss and reoperation.

paras: It is a short procedure done by a surgeon, with no skin removed. The crease shows immediately, with swelling settling over the following days to weeks. Some people have it redone if the crease loosens.
The crease may fade or loosen, requiring reoperation. Buried or exposed sutures can irritate or injure the cornea and have required removal. No randomised trials were found.

chain: Sutures bind lid skin to deeper tissue
angle.text: Buried stitches bind the lid skin to deeper tissue to form an upper-lid crease without an incision, giving larger, more defined eyes in a quick procedure. The crease is visible straight away, and reports describe it sometimes fading over time.

lead: Non-incisional double eyelid surgery, also called the buried-suture or suture-ligation method, creates an upper eyelid crease by passing sutures through the lid to bind the skin to deeper tissue such as the levator aponeurosis, without removing skin through an incision [1][2][3]. It is a variant of East Asian blepharoplasty, aimed at people who naturally lack a supratarsal crease [1].

Encyclopedia summaries say the method is quicker and associated with fewer complications than the incisional approach but that the crease can be static and may fade [1]. The published literature is largely retrospective and focuses on complications of the buried thread, such as suture exposure and corneal injury, and on crease loss and reoperation [2][4][5][6][7].
infobox: Crease loss, suture exposure, corneal injury [2][4][5]

paras: In suture methods one or more stitches are buried in the upper lid to create adhesion that forms a fold on opening the eye [1][2]. Variants include two-point and continuous buried sutures and techniques that incorporate orbicularis, levator and tarsus fixation [8]. The incisional alternative removes skin, fat and muscle and is described as giving a more dynamic and durable crease but a longer recovery, with lagophthalmos as a key risk [1].

Kotaro Mikamo performed the first reported double eyelid operation in Japan in 1896, and the procedure has since become among the most common aesthetic operations in East Asia, reported as the most common in Taiwan and South Korea [1][9].

A large Hiroshima-based institutional analysis examined factors associated with crease loss after hidden non-incisional suture surgery [5]. A 788-case cohort compared one-year outcomes in younger and older patients having continuous buried suture surgery [6], and a stratified analysis examined age-related variation in reoperation for suture loosening in two-point buried suture surgery [7]. A 4.5-year cohort assessed whether removing upper-lid fat altered the reoperation rate and long-term stability [10]. Another study found eyebrow position changes after double eyelid surgery related to pre-existing compensatory brow elevation [11].

Because a foreign suture is implanted, complications include suture exposure, granuloma, and ocular injury. A Japanese series of 210 upper eyelids in 116 patients examined removal techniques for suture-related complications [2]. A Chinese study of 12 patients described causes, management and prevention of corneal injury and other damage to the eye [3], and a study of 14 patients described misdiagnosis and treatment of corneal complications from suture exposure [4]. Two modified techniques were reported to decrease some suture-related complications [12].

Human studies are retrospective cohorts and case series [2][3][4][12][5][6][7][10]. No randomised controlled trials of non-incisional double eyelid surgery were found. Registered trials in the area concern ptosis surgery rather than crease formation.
